### Exact wording

English (as recorded here)

“Grace does not destroy nature, but perfects it.”

Latin

“Cum enim gratia non tollat naturam, sed perficiat.”

The sentence is subordinate in the Latin — “since grace does not destroy nature but perfects it” — inside a reply to an objection. The English rendering promotes it to a standalone assertion.

#### Forms in circulation that differ

-   “Grace does not destroy nature, but perfects it.”
-   “Grace perfects nature.”

### Attribution notes

Summa Theologiae I, q.1, a.8, reply to the second objection, where Aquinas is answering the charge that theology should not use philosophy. The sentence is his justification for borrowing from pagan philosophers: grace completes the natural powers it finds rather than replacing them. Quoted as a standalone maxim about grace it loses that it is, in place, an argument about what theologians may take from Aristotle.

#### About Thomas Aquinas

Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274) was the Dominican scholastic who synthesized Aristotelian philosophy with Christian theology in the Summa Theologiae and Summa contra Gentiles. Educated at Naples, Paris, and Cologne under Albert the Great, he taught in Paris and Italian studia.

### Interpretation

Aquinas is answering an objection that grace overrides or cancels human nature. His position is that grace presupposes nature: what is perfected must continue to exist and act, otherwise the word is being used loosely. The formula does real work in his system — it lets him hold that human capacities are genuinely damaged by sin without concluding they are destroyed, which is why moral effort and education still matter theologically.

#### Why it matters

It is also a constraint on any reform programme: if you want to change people, build on what they already are rather than treating their existing motives as obstacles to be replaced. Programs that assume the opposite tend to produce compliance, not change.

### Questions readers arrive with

#### What is the source of the quotation “Grace does not destroy nature, but perfects it.”?

“Grace does not destroy nature, but perfects it.” comes from Summa Theologiae I, q.1, a.8 ad, 2, attributed to Thomas Aquinas.

#### What does Thomas Aquinas mean by nature?

Nature may mean physical cosmos, living world, human nature, or a normative standard of what ought to be. Presocratics, Daoists, Stoics, and modern environmental thinkers share the word while disagreeing about its force. This passage enters that discussion through nature, reason.

#### Is the wording of this Thomas Aquinas quotation commonly changed?

The wording recorded here is “Grace does not destroy nature, but perfects it.” Forms in circulation that differ: Grace does not destroy nature, but perfects it. / Grace perfects nature. The Latin reads “Cum enim gratia non tollat naturam, sed perficiat.”

#### Is this quotation attributed correctly?

Summa Theologiae I, q.1, a.8, reply to the second objection, where Aquinas is answering the charge that theology should not use philosophy. The sentence is his justification for borrowing from pagan philosophers: grace completes the natural powers it finds rather than replacing them. Quoted as a standalone maxim about grace it loses that it is, in place, an argument about what theologians may take from Aristotle.
